name: Roentgenium

discovery.discoverer: Peter Armbruster, Sigurd Hofmann and team, GSI Darmstadt

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced only via particle accelerator fusion, atom by atom.
majorUses: No practical applications — pure superheavy-element research
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive; observed only as individual atoms with sub-second half-lives.
notableCharacteristics: Named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays and the first-ever recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics.
ncertRelevance: named after the discoverer of X-rays
whyHere: Predicted to sit in Group 11 below gold, roentgenium is theorized to show relativistic effects on its electrons even more extreme than gold's — potentially making it silvery rather than gold-coloured, though this has never been directly observed.
didYouKnow: Because relativistic effects get stronger with heavier nuclei, theoretical chemists predict roentgenium might actually look silvery rather than gold-coloured like the element directly above it — a genuinely counterintuitive prediction nobody has enough atoms to test.
genZNote: Predicted to NOT look gold-colored despite being right below gold, because relativity said so. Physics really said 'plot twist.'
